system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2172-06-16 06:48:00 to 2172-06-21 14:01:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a man with nonischemic cardiomyopathy and type 1 diabetes, was admitted for worsening shortness of breath after running out of Lasix. Initially treated for heart failure, he was found to have multifocal pneumonia on CT imaging. He developed septic shock, required intubation and mechanical ventilation, and was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. After extubation and clinical improvement, he was weaned off oxygen, regained mobility with a cane, and was discharged home. His kidney injury and hyperglycemia resolved, and mental health concerns were addressed with follow-up arranged. Cocaine use was noted, and counseling was provided.

fevers or other symptoms of systemic illness.  No peripheral 
edema, weight gain, medication noncompliance or dietary 
indescretion.

intubation, most recently on ___ at ___.  On recent

broad spectrum antibiotics and in less than 2 weeks, respiratory 
status and CXR had returned to baseline.

INDICATION:  Evaluation of patient with dyspnea with history of multifocal
pneumonia.

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior studies including chest radiograph from ___ and CTPA study from ___.

FINDINGS:  Severe bilateral diffuse parenchymal opacities are noted and appear
similar to that seen previously in ___.  Cardiomediastinal
silhouette remains stable.  No acute fractures are identified.

IMPRESSION:  Diffuse bilateral severe parenchymal opacities, similar to that
seen previously in ___ with multifocal pneumonia.  These findings
are more consistent with multifocal pneumonia, supperimposed  pulmonary edema
is possible.

SINGLE FRONTAL VIEW OF THE CHEST

REASON FOR EXAM:  Acute dyspnea.  Please evaluate lung abnormalities after
diuresis.

Comparison is made with prior study performed 6 hours earlier.

Diffuse bilateral opacities have mildly improved consistent with improving
moderate-to-severe pulmonary edema.  There are still  interstitial and
alveolar opacities diffusely distributed in the lungs, worse in the bases and
sparing the central portion of the right upper lobe.    Cardiomediastinal
contours are unchanged.  If any, there are small bilateral pleural effusions. 

IMPRESSION
Remaining opacities still could represent pulmonary edema or diffuse
multilobar pneumonia.   Continued followup is recommended.

HISTORY:  ___ man with history of coronary disease, diabetes, COPD,
and CHF, presents with chest pain, tachypnea, and shortness of breath. 
Progressively worsening over the last two days after he took crack cocaine. 
Concern for pneumonia versus hypersensitivity pneumonitis versus pulmonary
edema.

TECHNIQUE:  Volumetric, multidetector CT acquisition of the chest was
performed without intravenous or oral contrast.  Images are presented for
display in the axial plane at 1.25- and 5-mm collimation.  A series of
multiplanar reformation images were also submitted for review.

COMPARISON:  CT chest ___.

FINDINGS:
Visualized portions of the thyroid gland are unremarkable.  There is no
supracervical lymphadenopathy identified.  There is unchanged bulky
mediastinal lymphadenopathy however.  An aortopulmonary window lymph node
(2:20) measures 3.6 x 2.3 cm, a subcarinal lymph node measures 2.6 x 2.3 cm
(2:26).  Additional enlarged lymph nodes are seen in the prevascular and
pretracheal spaces (2:17, 18, 19).  The heart and great vessels are
unremarkable in appearance; however, the main pulmonary artery is somewhat
prominent measuring 3.8 cm.  The patient may be developing pulmonary arterial
hypertension.  Minor calcification of the aortic arch and coronary arteries is
seen.  There is mild pleural thickening or small pleural effusions
bilaterally. The airways are patent to a subsegmental level; however, in the
right lower lobe and the lingula, bronchi are seen extending at the periphery
of the lungs, suggesting an element of mild bronchiectasis.  There are
bilateral ground-glass opacities with areas of more confluent consolidation
also seen involving the right upper, left upper, and right middle lobes. The
left lower lobe is also involved as is the lingula. There is minimal volume
loss, most evident in the region of the lingula.  There is relative sparing of
the right upper lobe, however, this lung does not appear normal with decreased
opacity and decreased bronchovascular markings suggesting emphysematous change
A spiculated lesion in the right upper lobe is unchanged compared to the prior
study (4:67).  Bilateral pleural effusions are small and unchanged compared to
the prior study.

This study is not tailored for evaluation of the upper abdominal viscera;
however, upper portions of the liver and spleen appear unremarkable.  The
adrenal glands are not enlarged.

BONY STRUCTURES:  No destructive lytic or sclerotic bony lesions are seen.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Diffuse bilateral airspace opacities, predominantly of ground-glass
pattern, with areas of more confluent consolidations.  The distribution of
disease is nearly identical to the prior CT; however, it is noted that there
was interval resolution of these abnormalities (see chest radiograph ___.  Based on these findings, the pulmonary parenchymal abnormality is
felt likely to reflect re-exposure an agent causing a reactive
hypersensitivity pneumonitis or possibly an eosinophilic pneumonitis. 
Pulmonary edema is not considered likely given the distribution.  Atypical
infection such as PCP cannot be excluded.
2.  Bulky mediastinal lymphadenopathy is unchanged when compared to the prior
study and is likely reactive.
3.  Small bilateral pleural effusions, similar in appearance to the prior
study.  Small pericardial effusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Patel. You’re in the hospital because of shortness of breath. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I was okay until two days ago. I smoked crack, and then I started having trouble breathing. Felt like my chest was tight, like when my heart fails.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had this before, right? Similar episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, twice. Last time I had to be intubated. Thought it was heart failure again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is labored now. We’ve put you on BiPAP to help. Your chest X-ray shows diffuse opacities—fluid or inflammation in both lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it pneumonia again? Or my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. Your BNP is high—suggests heart strain. But the pattern on imaging isn’t typical for just fluid. We’re worried it could be ‘crack lung’—a reaction to smoking cocaine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Crack lung? I’ve never heard that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a type of lung injury from inhaling crack. Causes inflammation, not infection. It can look like pneumonia but clears quickly if you stop using.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So… did I do this to myself?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The timing suggests it’s related. But we’re treating both possibilities—your heart and lungs. We’ve started IV Lasix and nitroglycerin for your heart, and you’ve already made 2 liters of urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re improving a bit, but still need support. We’ll get a CT scan today to see more detail in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CT results. It shows ground-glass opacities throughout both lungs—very similar to your last scan, but the fact that it came back so fast after clearing suggests it’s not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. More consistent with hypersensitivity pneumonitis or crack lung. No signs of PCP or other infections. We’re not starting antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave one dose of IV steroids to reduce inflammation. But your blood sugar spiked, so we’re holding off. You’re on insulin now to manage it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugar’s usually okay. I take Lantus at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. You were on an insulin drip for a day, but we’re switching you back to your 40 units of Lantus tonight. Your sugars are coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your oxygen levels are better. We’ve weaned you from BiPAP to 6 liters on a nasal cannula, though you dipped into the 80s earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt okay then. Why did I desaturate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lungs are still inflamed. We’re keeping you on oxygen and monitoring. The crack lung theory fits—your body reacted strongly, but it’s starting to heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I just need to rest?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And stay off crack. That’s the most important thing. We’ve also started social work—they can help connect you with addiction support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I need help. I keep falling back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not judging. We want to keep you out of the hospital. Your sister is supportive—she can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a PICC line yesterday for better IV access. The first one was too low, so we adjusted it. It’s now in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it hurt? I don’t remember.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were sedated briefly. No complications. We’re using it to give meds and draw labs more easily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My breathing feels better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes! You’re on only 2 liters now, and your lung sounds are clearing. The inflammation is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want you on room air first and to make sure your heart is stable. You’ve lost about 2.7 liters of fluid—good for your heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Big improvement! You’ve been on room air all night with 96% oxygen. Your labs are better—white count down, no infection signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your BNP is still high, but your symptoms are better. We’re keeping you on Lasix, Lisinopril, and Metoprolol—same as home. No changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back on your Lantus. Sliding scale insulin as needed. Your sugars are in the 200s—higher than usual, but improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll check them at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day—we’re discharging you tomorrow. You’re walking, breathing on room air, and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s awesome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but with conditions. You must avoid all illicit drugs. This could happen again—and worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I want to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve set up follow-up with your primary doctor and social work will help with addiction services. Also, your hepatitis C needs monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t done anything about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need regular ultrasounds and blood tests. Treatment is possible, but we’ll discuss that with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re going home. Continue all your meds, especially Lasix, insulin, and inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no crack. I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, fever, or can’t keep meds down. You’re doing well—let’s keep it that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doc. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve got my sister helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great support. Keep using your inhalers and checking your sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And I’ll call for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re ready to go home. Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember—no smoking, no crack, and keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’m ready for a change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best news I’ve heard all day.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with nonischemic cardiomyopathy, type 1 diabetes, and a history of cocaine dependence was admitted for acute shortness of breath and chest pain following crack use. Initially managed for heart failure with diuresis and vasodilators, his respiratory status improved with BiPAP and fluid removal. Imaging revealed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities, with a pattern suggesting crack-induced lung injury or hypersensitivity pneumonitis rather than infection or pure pulmonary edema. He was treated with a single dose of steroids, which caused transient hyperglycemia managed with an insulin drip before returning to home insulin. Antibiotics were avoided due to lack of infection evidence. He weaned successfully from oxygen, stabilized on home heart and diabetes medications, and was discharged with instructions to avoid illicit substances, continue all medications, and follow up for addiction support and hepatitis C monitoring.
problems: Acute pulmonary syndrome (presumably related to crack-cocaine use)
Acute on chronic exacerbation of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy
